title: The Allocative Cost of War - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A new working paper by Gorodnichenko, Amann and Talavera uses comprehensive Ukrainian firm-level data from Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion to argue that war's economic cost runs mainly through a collapse in allocative productivity — the surviving economy working less efficiently — not just destroyed factors. The policy implication is that institutions enabling rapid reallocation under stress are critical to defense and national security.

themes.theme: Allocative efficiency as the hidden war cost

insights.claim: Modern war lowers output not only by destroying productive factors but by making the surviving economy work less efficiently, with Ukrainian firm-level data from 2022 documenting a dramatic collapse in allocative productivity.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Wartime GDP damage estimates built only on destroyed capital understate the hit; reconstruction and recovery models should price the misallocation channel.
insights.quote: modern war lowers output not only by destroying productive factors, but also by making the surviving economy work less efficiently
insights.locator: Why is war so economically costly?

insights.claim: Identification exploits spatial heterogeneity across Ukrainian districts and comparisons with the 2014 Russian aggression and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, isolating mechanisms including war intensity, internal displacement, reallocation and macroeconomic instability.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Benchmarking war shocks against the GFC gives a comparative scale for how severe wartime misallocation is relative to a known financial crisis.
insights.locator: To sharpen identification and explore key mechanisms

insights.claim: Restoring allocative efficiency and pre-building institutional arrangements that facilitate rapid reallocation in times of stress is framed as critical for sustaining economic capacity, defense and national security.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Argues defense-industrial resilience is an institutional/reallocation problem as much as a spending problem — relevant to how European rearmament budgets get judged.
insights.quote: restoring allocative efficiency–and preparing institutional arrangements that facilitate rapid reallocation in times of stress–is critical for sustaining economic capacity, defense, and national security
